n: Cathedral Basilica of St. John the Baptist
s: An old diocese, now answering to Atlanta
w: Bishop Stephen D. Parkes now leads the Diocese of Savannah from its mother church downtown, a Catholic seat covering all of southern Georgia. It answers up the chain to the Archdiocese of Atlanta these days - proof that even old dioceses shuffle around under new management.
_facts: Cathedral Basilica of Saint John the Baptist is the mother church of the Diocese of Savannah
the diocese covers southern Georgia
it is a suffragan diocese of the Archdiocese of Atlanta
current bishop is Stephen D. Parkes

s: A West Point rookie's fort that fell without a fight
w: A West Point grad barely out of school engineered this river fort in 1808 to guard Savannah from attack by sea. It never got the chance - when Sherman took the city by land in 1864, the fort fell almost immediately. Restored in the 1970s, it is now a National Historic Landmark.
_facts: built 1808-1812, engineered by William McRee fresh out of West Point
one of three Confederate forts defending Savannah in the Civil War
captured almost immediately when Sherman took Savannah by land in December 1864
restored in the 1970s, declared a National Historic Landmark in 2000

s: A monument, and the rare railing still around it
w: A Polish cavalry commander who died just outside these city limits during the siege of Savannah gets a 19th-century monument on Monterey Square, not far from where he fell. It is one of only two monuments in the city still ringed by its original iron railing - the other stands in Forsyth Park.
_facts: 19th-century monument to Casimir Pulaski, who died during the siege of Savannah
stands in Monterey Square on Bull Street
one of only two Savannah monuments that still has its original railing, the other being the Civil War Memorial in Forsyth Park

s: From British studies center to art museum
w: What began in 2002 as a British-American studies center reopened in 2011 as something else entirely - a teaching museum wrapped around an 86-foot glass-and-steel lantern, its galleries running from haute couture to an Andre Leon Talley gallery named for the late Vogue editor. Over 4,500 pieces, still growing.
_facts: founded 2002, originally the Earle W. Newton Center for British American Studies
reopened October 29, 2011 after extensive rehabilitation
86-foot steel and glass lantern entrance
collection of more than 4,500 pieces including the Andre Leon Talley Gallery

s: A parade ground turned into thirty acres of park
w: Thirty acres in the heart of the historic district began life as a military parade ground before Savannah handed it over to fountains and footpaths. Its Fragrant Garden was built for blind visitors to navigate by scent alone, and the lawns still host benefit concerts for the whole city to wander into.
_facts: formerly known as Forsyth Place and the Military Parade Ground
30 acres in the Savannah Historic District
includes a Fragrant Garden built for the blind
hosts benefit concerts

s: The South's first public art museum, in a mansion
w: The South's first public art museum opened in 1886 inside a Savannah heiress's Regency mansion, willed to the city by Mary Telfair. It now spans three buildings, including the Owens-Thomas House and its surviving slave quarters - two National Historic Landmarks beside a Moshe Safdie wing built decades later.
_facts: first public art museum in the Southern United States, founded through the bequest of Mary Telfair
opened 1886 in the Telfair family's Regency mansion, Telfair Academy
also includes the Owens-Thomas House & Slave Quarters, a National Historic Landmark
third building is the Jepson Center for the Arts, designed by Moshe Safdie, completed 2006
